prompt: You run four client projects. Monday morning brings these items. Rank them, most urgent first.

task.prompt: You run four client projects. Monday morning brings these items. Rank them, most urgent first.

items.label: Production checkout is down on Project A's live app
Project B's client needs a go/no-go decision for tomorrow's release
Project C's sprint planning is this afternoon and the backlog is not refined
Project D's client asked for a monthly report due Friday
A team member asked for feedback on their career plan

task.explanation: Live outage first, then a time-boxed release decision, then today's planning, then a report due later in the week; the career talk matters but can be scheduled.

prompt: Context switching has a cost. Using the common rule of thumb below, estimate productive time for a developer split across projects.

task.prompt: Context switching has a cost. Using the common rule of thumb below, estimate productive time for a developer split across projects.

fields.label: Productive hours per project in a 40-hour week with 3 projects
Productive hours on one project if dedicated

task.explanation: With 3 projects, 60% of 40 = 24 productive hours, or 8 per project, compared with 40 on one project.

prompt: A PM's weekly plan across three projects. Mark the practices that will cause trouble.

task.prompt: A PM's weekly plan across three projects. Mark the practices that will cause trouble.

segments.text: Each project has a fixed weekly status slot with its client.
I review all three RAID logs every Monday.
I promised all three clients the same senior developer for next week.
segments.issue: Over-committing a shared resource guarantees a conflict; resolve allocation before promising.

segments.text: Project priorities are agreed with my director when they conflict.
I answer every Slack message within five minutes, all day.
segments.issue: Constant interruption destroys focus; set response windows and escalation channels.

segments.text: I keep a single calendar with all project milestones.
I skip retrospectives on the smaller projects to save time.
segments.issue: Small projects benefit from lightweight retros too; skipping them hides recurring problems.

segments.text: Client decisions are logged in each project's decision log.

prompt: Two of your projects need the same iOS developer next week for urgent fixes. Both clients have been promised quick turnarounds.

task.prompt: Two of your projects need the same iOS developer next week for urgent fixes. Both clients have been promised quick turnarounds.

steps.question: What is your first step?
options: Split the developer 50/50
Give the developer to the louder client
Ask the developer to work both full-time
Assess each fix's business impact and deadline, then agree priority with your resource manager
steps.explanation: Priority is a business decision made with facts, not volume or overtime.

steps.question: Project A's fix goes first. What do you tell Project B's client?
options: Nothing until the developer is free
A realistic new date and any interim workaround, before they chase you
That the developer is sick
That the fix is in progress

prompt: Order the steps to set up a weekly portfolio review for the projects you manage.

task.prompt: Order the steps to set up a weekly portfolio review for the projects you manage.

items.label: Agree a common status format for every project
Collect updates from each project before the meeting
Review cross-project risks and shared resources first
Record decisions and communicate to teams and clients

task.explanation: Comparable data, gathered in advance, reviewed for cross-project conflicts, decided, then communicated.

prompt: You manage five projects and are working 60-hour weeks. Quality of your reporting is slipping.

task.prompt: You manage five projects and are working 60-hour weeks. Quality of your reporting is slipping.

steps.question: What is the best first move?
options: List where your time goes, then delegate or standardise the repeatable parts (reports, minutes, ticket hygiene)
Work weekends until things calm down
Stop sending status reports
Drop the smallest client
steps.explanation: Find the waste before cutting value or burning out.

steps.question: Your director asks what would help. What do you ask for?
options: Nothing; you will manage
A bigger bonus
A cap on concurrent projects or a junior PM to own day-to-day coordination on two of them
Removal of all client meetings
steps.explanation: Capacity problems need capacity solutions, stated concretely.

prompt: Why is limiting the number of projects a person works on at once important?

options: Clients dislike shared staff
Context switching wastes time and raises errors, so fewer concurrent projects deliver more
It makes timesheets simpler
It lowers salaries
mcq.explanation: Each extra concurrent project adds switching overhead; focus improves flow across the portfolio.

prompt: Two projects you manage both claim top priority. Who should decide?

options: The person with portfolio authority, usually a director, using agreed criteria such as revenue, risk and commitments
Whichever client calls first
The developers
The PM alone, based on preference
mcq.explanation: Cross-project priority is a business decision; the PM brings the facts to the person accountable.

prompt: What makes a single status format across all your projects useful?

options: It looks more professional
Clients require it
It lets you and leadership compare projects quickly and spot trouble
It removes the need for project-specific detail
mcq.explanation: Comparable status turns many projects into a portfolio view; project detail still lives in each project.
